title: Regional throughput reservations and graceful siphon for multi-zone dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem statement: Customers running Dedicated capacity in multiple regions/zones need predictable per-region throughput guarantees while still allowing capacity to be reclaimed for global spikes. Current Dedicated pools can be pinned to regions but lack a first-class model for reserving a percentage of capacity for regional SLAs and a safe, low-latency mechanism to siphon traffic during evacuation or maintenance windows.
acceptance_criteria: Controller accepts a new pool policy object that specifies per-region reserved throughput (tokens/sec or rps equivalent) and a siphon behavior window
When a region enters evacuation or loses nodes, traffic is gradually moved out according to the siphon window and QoS tiers; p95 latency must not regress >10% for critical customers during canary
Autoscaler respects reserved throughput and will not scale down below reservation unless overridden by an operator flag
Routing decisions documented and observable in Console: per-route breakdown showing reserved vs. opportunistic capacity usage
End-to-end e2e test that simulates zonal drain and validates graceful siphon without violating data-residency constraints for labelled workloads
tasks: Design API: poolPolicy {regionReservations: [{region, minThroughput, priority}], siphonWindowSec, allowBorrowing:false/true}
Runtime: implement reservation-aware bin-packing in scheduler and a siphon state machine for each pool
Autoscaler: add lower bound guard that respects reservations and a soft-borrow path when global utilization > threshold
Routing: extend smart-router to consult reservations and fallback lanes (local -> adjacent-region -> regional-fallback) with telemetry tags
Console: dashboard card for reservations, live siphon progress, and per-route latency/cost impact
E2E: chaos test for node loss and scheduled maintenance; unit tests for policy parsing
Docs: PRD + public docs describing reservation semantics, billing implications, and operator runbook
notes: Edge cases considered: 1) Mixed workloads with data-residency labels (must never cross certain geofences), 2) Sudden global spike where reserved capacity might be borrowed temporarily—behavior must be explicit and auditable, 3) Handling model-variant incompatibilities across regions (different quantization/hardware profiles).
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (design & API) -> Phase 2 (scheduler + autoscaler changes) -> Phase 3 (router + console + canary) -> Phase 4 (docs + wider rollout). Target small canary with two mid-size customers in one region pair before org-wide release.
rollout_plan: Canary group: 2 customers (non-regulated) using a single dedicated pool with us-west/us-east pair. Enable regionReservations with conservative minThroughput values. Monitor p95/p99 latency, dropped requests, and reserve utilization. After 2 weeks with no regressions, expand to 10 customers and run data-residency test cases. Final release gated by SLO compliance and security review signoff.
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Over-reservation reduces global capacity and increases cost - Mitigation: provide operator-visible borrow thresholds and automatic reclamation policies
Risk: Incorrect siphon logic causes traffic spikes to adjacent regions - Mitigation: rate-limited siphon and staged drain (10s/60s/5m windows) plus circuit-breaker
Risk: Data-residency labels accidentally bypassed during failover - Mitigation: strict geofence matcher in router and unit-tests in admission controller
outstanding_questions: What billing model for reserved throughput—flat fee vs. min-usage credit? Need PM guidance
Should borrowing be billable at a premium rate to discourage frequent borrowing?
How do we express multi-tenant pools where some tenants have stricter residency constraints?
